overview: This domain is about making sure every person and every system that touches an organization's data is known, proven and limited to what it needs. Topic 3.1 follows an identity from the day it is created, through job changes and reviews, to the day it is removed, and covers how people and systems prove who they are. Topic 3.2 covers the rules that limit what an identity can do once it is in: least privilege, separation of duties and the main access control models. As an entry-level practitioner, you will often run these processes, notice when they break and report gaps to the right owner.
analogy: Think of a hotel. The front desk checks a guest's ID before handing over a key card, and the card opens only that guest's room and the gym. Staff cards open more doors, but the master card is kept in the safe and signed out. When a guest changes rooms, the old card stops working; at checkout it is canceled. The delivery robot gets its own card that opens only the service lift, and each night someone checks which cards are still active.

topics.overview: The identity life cycle is the path every account follows: a role is defined, the account is created with approved access, access is adjusted and checked as duties change, and the account is removed when no longer needed. This topic also covers how people and systems prove who they are, and the frameworks and tools that run the cycle at scale.
can_do: Put joiner, mover and leaver tasks in the right order, including removing old access when someone changes jobs
Tell true multi-factor authentication from two checks of the same factor, and name phishing-resistant options
Explain what an access review checks, who should sign it off and what happens to access nobody confirms
Manage service accounts, bots and AI agents through the same life cycle as people

subtopics.name: Identities, Accounts and the Life Cycle
subtopics.definition: An identity represents one person or system; accounts are its logins on specific systems. The identity life cycle manages both, from creation to removal.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Access can only be controlled and traced when every account belongs to a known identity with an owner. Orphaned, shared and forgotten accounts are easy doors for attackers and leave nobody accountable.
how_it_works: Identification is the claim, such as a username; authentication proves the claim; authorization then decides what the identity may do.
Each person gets one unique identity, so every logged action traces back to someone.
The joiner, mover and leaver stages create access, adjust it when duties change and remove it at exit.
Access reviews run alongside the whole cycle, confirming each account and right is still needed.
A trusted source, usually the human resources (HR) system, triggers each stage so changes are not missed.

types.meaning: Everyday access for one named person
Administrator or root rights that can change systems, security settings or other users' access
Used by an application or process rather than a person
One login used by several people; it hides who acted, so avoid it
Short-term access for a visitor, contractor or project, with an end date

illustration.caption: Each stage is triggered by a trusted record, such as an HR start, transfer or exit. Reviews run under the whole cycle to catch anything a stage missed.

subtopics.example: At a regional bus company, a new dispatcher, Sam, starts on Monday. The HR start record creates Sam's account with the dispatcher role. A year later Sam moves to payroll and the dispatch rights are removed; when Sam leaves, the exit record disables the account that day. Each month Lee, a junior analyst, matches the account list to HR records and reports accounts with no current owner to the IAM team.

review: Match the active account list against current HR records
Confirm every shared or service account has a named owner
evidence: Directory export showing each account's owner and last sign-in
HR joiner, mover and leaver reports for the same period
audit_focus.recommend: Report orphaned or ownerless accounts to the IAM team and the system owner instead of deleting them yourself.
audit_focus.decides: The system owner decides whether an unowned account is kept or removed

subtopics.isaca_rule: Every account needs one identity and one accountable owner. When a trusted record, not someone's memory, triggers each stage, access stays accurate. Treat any account nobody can explain as a risk to report.

exam_traps.trap: Typing a username proves who someone is.
exam_traps.why: A username is only identification, a claim. Proof comes from authentication, such as a password plus a second factor.

exam_traps.trap: A shared team login is fine when everyone on the team needs the same access.
exam_traps.why: Shared logins hide who did what. Give each person their own account with the same role instead.

key_terms.definition: Claiming an identity, for example by typing a username, before any proof is checked.
An active account whose owner has left or cannot be found.
The three events that trigger access changes: starting, changing jobs and leaving.

subtopics.memory_aid: Claim, prove, permit: identification, authentication, authorization.

subtopics.name: Defining Roles and Entitlements
subtopics.definition: Defining roles means grouping the access a job needs into a named role, so people get a standard, approved set of entitlements instead of one-off grants.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Clear roles make provisioning fast and consistent and make reviews possible. Without them, access gets copied from a coworker and people quietly collect rights they never needed.
how_it_works: Start from job duties: list the tasks a role performs, then the systems and permissions each task needs.
The business or data owner approves what each role contains; IT builds the role in the systems.
Keep roles broad enough to manage but narrow enough for least privilege.
Check each role for separation of duties conflicts before it is approved.
Handle one person's extra need through a time-limited request, not by widening the role for everyone.
subtopics.example: A city library defines a circulation clerk role: check items in and out and view borrower contact details, but not waive fines. The branch manager approves it. When a supervisor asks to give one clerk fine-waiving rights for a week, Priya, a junior IAM analyst, opens a temporary access request with an end date and routes it to the branch manager instead of editing the role.

review: Trace each permission in a role back to a task it supports
Use time-limited requests with end dates for one-off needs
evidence: Role catalog listing each role, its permissions and its owner
Approval records showing who signed off each role change
audit_focus.recommend: Raise any role that mixes conflicting duties with the role owner and the security team before anyone is assigned it.
audit_focus.decides: The role's business owner signs off its contents

subtopics.isaca_rule: Roles come from duties, not from copying a coworker. The owner of the data approves the role, and IT carries it out. One person's unusual need is a time-limited exception, not a reason to widen the role.

exam_traps.trap: Copy a coworker's access for a new hire on the same team.
exam_traps.why: The coworker may hold leftover rights from past jobs. Starting from the approved role gives only what the job needs.

exam_traps.trap: IT should decide what each role can access, because IT manages the systems.
exam_traps.why: IT builds and runs roles, but the business or data owner knows what the work needs and is accountable for approving it.

key_terms.definition: A single permission or access right, such as read access to a folder or the right to approve payments.
Having so many narrow or custom roles that nobody can manage or review them.
Basic access every staff member gets on day one, such as email and the staff intranet.

subtopics.name: Provisioning and Identity Proofing
subtopics.definition: Provisioning creates an account and grants its approved access. Identity proofing first checks that the person is who they claim to be before any credentials are issued.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Getting access right on day one is far easier than fixing it later. Weak proofing lets an impostor be enrolled as a real employee, holding legitimate credentials from the start.
how_it_works: A request comes from a trusted source, such as an HR start record, not an informal email or chat message.
The manager or data owner approves the access, and the approver should not be the person who builds it.
Identity proofing checks evidence, such as photo ID matched to the person, with stronger checks for riskier access.
First credentials go through a channel already on file, work only once and must be replaced at first sign-in.
Automated provisioning from the HR system to the directory reduces errors and leaves a clear record.
subtopics.example: A logistics firm hires a remote driver coordinator, Jordan. Before activating the account, Mei, the help desk technician, holds a video call in which Jordan shows a photo ID that Mei compares with the HR file. The account is created from the HR record with the coordinator role only. When Jordan asks for the setup link at a personal email address, Mei sends it to the work phone on file instead.

review: Confirm the request matches an HR record before creating anything
Grant only the approved role, then confirm with the requester
evidence: The access request ticket with the owner's approval
Provisioning log showing who created the account and when
audit_focus.recommend: Send unusual requests, such as urgent access with no HR record, to your supervisor or the IAM team before acting.
audit_focus.decides: The hiring manager signs off a newcomer's starting access

subtopics.isaca_rule: No record, no account. Access starts from an approved request and the smallest role that fits. Prove the person before handing over credentials, and send those credentials through a channel already on file.

exam_traps.trap: An urgent request from a senior manager is a good reason to skip approval.
exam_traps.why: Urgency and authority are classic social engineering pressure. Follow the process and escalate; a real manager can approve properly.

exam_traps.trap: Give new staff broad access first and trim it later.
exam_traps.why: Later rarely comes, and the extra access is live from day one. Start small and add access through requests.

key_terms.definition: How strongly a claimed identity was checked at enrollment; NIST SP 800-63A-4 defines three levels.
Linking a verified person to their first authenticators, such as a password and a security key.
The automated steps that turn an approved request into accounts and rights across systems.

subtopics.name: Authentication Factors and MFA
subtopics.definition: Authentication factors are categories of proof: something you know, something you have and something you are. Multi-factor authentication (MFA) combines at least two different categories.
subtopics.why_it_matters: One factor can fail on its own, and stolen passwords are common. Requiring a second, different category means an attacker must steal two unlike things, which is much harder.
how_it_works: MFA needs factors from different categories; a password plus a security question is still single-factor.
Two-step checks are only MFA when the steps come from different categories.
Some texts add location or behavior as factors; NIST treats them as supporting signals, not separate factors.
Biometric readers can wrongly accept an impostor or wrongly reject a real user, so both error rates matter.
A device factor is often unlocked by a PIN or fingerprint, which adds a second category on the device.

types.meaning: A secret held in memory: password, passphrase or PIN
An object you hold: a phone with an authenticator app, a security key or a smart card
A body trait: fingerprint, face, iris or voice

subtopics.example: A dental clinic's new staff portal asks for a password and then the name of each user's first pet. The practice manager calls this MFA. Alex, the clinic's IT assistant, points out that both are things you know, so it is one factor used twice. Alex writes up a code from an authenticator app or a security key as the second step and sends it to the practice manager.

review: Name the category of each sign-in step before calling it MFA
Test that the second factor is required, not just offered
evidence: Sign-in policy settings showing which methods each group must use
Sign-in logs showing which method each user actually used
audit_focus.recommend: Report systems that accept a password alone for remote or administrator access to the security team.
audit_focus.decides: The system owner sets the required methods, within security policy

subtopics.isaca_rule: Count categories, not steps. MFA means at least two of know, have and are. Two checks of the same kind, however many prompts, are still one factor.

exam_traps.trap: A password and a PIN together count as MFA.
exam_traps.why: Both are things you know. MFA needs a different category, such as a phone app (have) or a fingerprint (are).

exam_traps.trap: Biometrics are a perfect factor because no two fingerprints match.
exam_traps.why: Readers make errors both ways, and a copied biometric cannot be changed like a password. It works best combined with another factor.

key_terms.definition: Any sign-in with two checks in sequence; it is MFA only when the checks use different factor categories.
How often a biometric reader wrongly lets in an impostor; the security failure.
How often a biometric reader wrongly turns away the genuine user; the convenience failure.

subtopics.memory_aid: Know, have, are: pick two different ones.

subtopics.name: Phishing-Resistant MFA and Passkeys
subtopics.definition: Phishing-resistant authentication ties each login to the genuine website or app, so a fake site cannot capture and reuse it. FIDO2 security keys and passkeys are common examples.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Attackers relay one-time codes through fake login pages in real time and flood users with push prompts. MFA that a person can be tricked into handing over only slows attackers down.
how_it_works: Passkeys and FIDO2 keys use a key pair; the private key stays with the user and signs a challenge from the real site.
The browser and authenticator check the site's address, so a look-alike domain gets nothing it can reuse.
Codes sent by text or shown in an app can be typed into a fake page and replayed by the attacker.
Repeated push prompts can wear a user down until they approve; number matching reduces this.
NIST SP 800-63B-4 lists text and voice codes as restricted and requires phishing-resistant options at higher assurance levels.
Synced passkeys copy across a user's devices; device-bound keys never leave one device.

rows.label: Factor category
cells: Have (the phone number)
Have (the phone app)
Have, usually unlocked by a PIN or fingerprint

rows.label: Stops a fake login page?
cells: No; the code can be relayed
No; a tired user may approve
Yes; it works only on the real site

rows.label: Main weakness
cells: SIM swap and interception
Repeated prompts until someone taps approve
A lost device needs a tested recovery method

subtopics.example: At a credit union, a teller, Ravi, gets five sign-in prompts on their phone at 2 a.m. without trying to log in. Half asleep, Ravi almost taps approve. Instead, Ravi denies each prompt and reports it to the security team straight away, so the team can reset the password that someone has clearly stolen.

review: Deny any sign-in prompt you did not start, then report it
Register a backup authenticator so a lost key does not block work
evidence: Sign-in logs showing bursts of denied or unexpected push prompts
List of administrator accounts still using text-message codes
audit_focus.recommend: Report unexpected MFA prompts to the security team at once, because they mean the password is probably known.
audit_focus.decides: Security leaders set which MFA methods each group of users must use

subtopics.isaca_rule: Not all MFA is equal: any code or approval a person can be tricked into giving away can be phished. For administrators and other high-risk users, prefer site-bound methods such as passkeys.

exam_traps.trap: Any MFA stops phishing.
exam_traps.why: Codes and push approvals can be relayed through a fake page or approved by a tired user. Only site-bound methods such as passkeys resist that relay.

exam_traps.trap: An unexpected MFA prompt is just a system glitch.
exam_traps.why: A prompt you did not trigger usually means someone has your password. Deny it and report it so the password can be reset.

key_terms.definition: An open standard (WebAuthn plus CTAP) for signing in with public-key cryptography instead of a shared secret.
An attack that sends push prompts again and again until the user approves one to make them stop.
A push setting where the user types the number shown on the login screen, so a blind approval fails.

subtopics.name: Passwords and Modern Password Policy
subtopics.definition: A password policy sets how passwords are created, checked and stored. Current NIST guidance favors length and breach screening over character-mix rules and forced scheduled changes.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Old rules pushed people toward predictable patterns like Summer2026! and sticky notes. Modern rules make passwords harder to guess and easier to live with, and the password is often still the first factor.
how_it_works: NIST SP 800-63B-4 sets at least 15 characters when a password is the only factor, and at least 8 when it is part of MFA.
Allow long passphrases of at least 64 characters, with spaces and pasting, so password managers work.
Check new passwords against lists of breached and common passwords, and reject any match.
Do not demand character mixes or calendar-based changes; require a change when there is evidence of compromise.
Limit failed attempts, and do not use password hints or security questions.
Store passwords only as salted, deliberately slow hashes, never as plain text.
subtopics.example: A school district's policy still demands eight characters, a symbol and a change every 60 days. Help desk calls spike after each change, and many new passwords just bump a number at the end. Tomas, a junior analyst, compares the policy with NIST SP 800-63B-4 and writes a summary for the IT manager: longer passphrases, breach screening, no scheduled changes and MFA for staff.

review: Compare the written policy with current NIST password guidance
Force a reset at once when there is evidence of a breach
evidence: Directory password settings for length, lockout and expiry
Breached-password screening results for newly set passwords
audit_focus.recommend: Send suggested policy changes to the policy owner; do not change live password settings on your own.
audit_focus.decides: The policy owner, such as the security manager, approves password rule changes

subtopics.isaca_rule: Length beats complexity, and screening beats expiry. Change a password when there is a reason, such as a breach, not because the calendar says so. A strong password is still one factor, so pair it with MFA.

exam_traps.trap: Requiring a password change every 90 days keeps accounts safe.
exam_traps.why: Scheduled changes lead to small, predictable edits. Current NIST guidance calls for a change on evidence of compromise, plus screening against breached lists.

exam_traps.trap: More character rules always make stronger passwords.
exam_traps.why: Composition rules produce patterns like Password1!. Length and blocking known-breached passwords add far more real strength.

key_terms.definition: A long password made of several words, easier to remember and harder to guess than a short complex one.
An app that creates, stores and fills a unique strong password for every site.
Trying username and password pairs leaked from one site on other sites; it works when people reuse passwords.

subtopics.name: Single Sign-On and Federation
subtopics.definition: Single sign-on (SSO) lets a user sign in once to an identity provider and reach many applications; federation extends that trust to applications run by other organizations.
subtopics.why_it_matters: SSO means fewer passwords to reuse and one place to turn access off. It also concentrates risk: one stolen SSO login, or one identity provider outage, affects every connected application.
how_it_works: The identity provider authenticates the user, then sends the application a signed statement that the application trusts.
The application never sees the user's password; it relies on the identity provider's statement.
Strong MFA at the identity provider protects every connected application at once.
Federation lets a partner's or cloud provider's application accept sign-ins from your identity provider.
Disabling a user at the identity provider stops new sign-ins, but open application sessions may last until revoked or expired.

rows.label: Main job
cells: Web sign-on, often for business applications
Sign-on for web and mobile apps
Lets an app reach data on a user's behalf

rows.label: Proves who the user is?
cells: Yes
Yes, by adding an identity layer to OAuth 2.0
No; it grants limited access, not identity

rows.label: What it sends
cells: Signed assertions
ID tokens plus access tokens
Scoped access tokens

subtopics.example: A charity uses SSO for email, file sharing and its donor database. A volunteer coordinator, Nia, leaves on Friday. Chris, the IT volunteer, disables Nia's account at the identity provider, then checks the donor database and finds Nia still signed in from a home laptop. Chris ends that session from the database's admin console and notes it on the leaver ticket.

review: Confirm MFA is enforced at the identity provider for every user
End open application sessions when an account is disabled
evidence: Identity provider sign-in logs for failed and unusual sign-ins
Applications that still allow a local password beside SSO
audit_focus.recommend: Report applications that bypass SSO with local logins to the application owner and the IAM team.
audit_focus.decides: Application owners decide, with the security team, which applications must use SSO

subtopics.isaca_rule: SSO moves the front door to one place, so guard that door hardest: strong MFA, monitoring and a plan for outages. Turning off the SSO account starts removal; ending sessions and tokens finishes it.

exam_traps.trap: SSO is less secure than separate logins because one password opens everything.
exam_traps.why: SSO concentrates risk, but with strong MFA at the identity provider it usually beats many reused passwords. The answer is protecting the identity provider, not avoiding SSO.

exam_traps.trap: OAuth 2.0 is a login protocol that proves who the user is.
exam_traps.why: OAuth 2.0 grants an app limited access to resources. Proof of identity comes from OpenID Connect, built on top of it.

key_terms.definition: The trusted service that authenticates users and vouches for them to applications.
The application that accepts the identity provider's statement instead of checking the password itself; also called a service provider.
An agreement letting separate organizations or systems trust each other's sign-ins.

subtopics.name: Adaptive Authentication and AI Behavior Analysis
subtopics.definition: Adaptive, or risk-based, authentication adjusts sign-in checks to the risk of each attempt, often using AI models that learn each user's normal behavior and flag unusual activity.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Fixed rules miss stolen credentials used in a normal-looking way. Behavior analysis can catch an attacker who has the right password, and spares low-risk users extra prompts.
how_it_works: The system scores each sign-in using signals such as device, location, time, network and usage patterns.
Low risk passes quietly, medium risk asks for a stronger factor, and high risk is blocked and sent for review.
Behavior analytics builds a baseline of normal activity for people, devices and service accounts, then flags departures from it.
Models make mistakes both ways and drift as habits change, so people must review alerts and tune thresholds.
Behavior data is personal data: collect only what is needed and tell users how it is used.
subtopics.example: A hospital's sign-in system flags a nurse, Dana, signing in from another country ten minutes after Dana badged into the ward. The AI model blocks the attempt and asks for a security key, which the attacker lacks. Kim, a security operations analyst, sees the alert, confirms with the ward that Dana is on shift and follows the playbook: force a password reset and open an incident ticket.

review: Triage risk alerts with the playbook, highest scores first
Record false positives so the model and thresholds can be tuned
evidence: Risk-scored sign-in events with the signals behind each score
History of alerts marked true or false positive
audit_focus.recommend: Escalate a confirmed account takeover to the incident response team rather than only resetting the password.
audit_focus.decides: The security manager approves risk thresholds and what each level triggers

subtopics.isaca_rule: AI scoring is a smart extra layer, not a replacement for strong factors or human judgment. Use it to step up checks when risk rises, keep people reviewing its alerts and treat behavior data as personal data.

exam_traps.trap: Once AI behavior analysis is running, MFA is no longer needed.
exam_traps.why: Risk scoring decides when to ask for more proof; it still needs strong factors to ask for. Models also miss attacks and raise false alarms.

exam_traps.trap: Every AI risk alert means the account is compromised.
exam_traps.why: Travel, new devices and VPNs cause false positives. Check each alert against facts, such as the person's schedule, before acting.

key_terms.definition: Tools that learn normal behavior for users, devices and accounts and alert on unusual activity.
Asking for a stronger or extra factor only when a sign-in or action looks risky.
Sign-ins from two places too far apart for one person to travel between in the time shown.

subtopics.name: Movers and Privilege Creep
subtopics.definition: A mover is a person whose job or duties change. Handling a mover adds the new role's access and removes old access the new role does not need.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Movers are the stage most often missed. People who keep old rights at each move build up privilege creep, which breaks least privilege and can create separation of duties conflicts.
how_it_works: An HR transfer record triggers the mover process, just as a start date triggers provisioning.
Remove old access at the move, not at the next review; keep it only with approval and an end date.
Check the combined old and new rights for conflicts, such as raising and approving the same payment.
The new manager approves new access; the old manager confirms what can be removed.
Acting and temporary assignments get access that expires automatically.
subtopics.example: Ana moves from accounts payable to purchasing at a hotel group. Purchasing access is added, but nobody removes Ana's payment approval rights, so Ana can now raise a purchase order and pay it. Jun, an IAM analyst, spots the conflict in the weekly mover report, opens a ticket to remove the old rights and flags the conflict to the finance owner the same day.

review: Compare a mover's old and new rights after each job change
Set end dates on any old access kept for handover
evidence: HR transfer records matched to access changes in the directory
Users holding rights from more than one role
audit_focus.recommend: Raise conflicting old and new rights with the data owner and the IAM team before the move completes.
audit_focus.decides: The data owner decides whether any old access may stay, and for how long

subtopics.isaca_rule: A transfer is a leaver and a joiner at once: remove the old, then add the new. Access that is not removed at the move tends to stay forever.

exam_traps.trap: Movers keep their old access in case their old team needs help.
exam_traps.why: That builds privilege creep and can create conflicts. Handover access, if truly needed, is approved separately and expires on a set date.

exam_traps.trap: The next access review will catch leftover mover access, so it can wait.
exam_traps.why: Reviews are a backstop, often months apart. Removing old access at the move closes the gap the day it opens.

key_terms.definition: The slow buildup of access as people change jobs and keep rights they no longer need.
Old-role access kept briefly, with approval and an end date, to finish passing work on.

subtopics.name: Access Reviews and Recertification
subtopics.definition: An access review is a regular check, by someone who knows the work, that each account and right is still needed. Recertification is the formal sign-off of that check.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Process gaps happen: a missed mover, an emergency grant never removed, a forgotten test account. Reviews catch what slipped through and give evidence that access is under control.
how_it_works: The reviewer is the manager or data owner who knows what the work needs, not the person whose access is reviewed.
Reviews follow a set schedule, and run more often for privileged and sensitive access.
Each right is confirmed, changed or removed; access nobody confirms is removed, not left in place.
Service accounts and bot identities are reviewed too, each through its named owner.
The review ends when every removal is done in the systems, not when the form is signed.

types.meaning: A manager confirms the access of each person on their team
A system or data owner confirms who may reach their asset
A review triggered by a job change, incident or reorganization rather than the calendar

subtopics.example: A university's research database owner, Dr. Okafor, receives the quarterly review list and approves all 300 accounts in four minutes. Riley, the junior security analyst running the review, notices the speed and finds 20 accounts belonging to students who have graduated. Riley sends those 20 names back to the owner, asks for a decision on each and tracks the removals until the system shows them gone.

review: Route each review line to the manager or owner accountable for it
Follow every removal decision until the system shows it done
evidence: Review sign-offs with the time each reviewer spent
Before-and-after account lists proving removals happened
audit_focus.recommend: Report overdue reviews, or reviews approved without reading, to the review owner's manager or the security team.
audit_focus.decides: The data or system owner certifies who keeps access

subtopics.isaca_rule: A review counts only when the right person reviews, decides on every line and the removals actually happen. If nobody confirms an access right, remove it.

exam_traps.trap: Users should review their own access, since they know what they use.
exam_traps.why: Self-review is a conflict of interest. The manager or data owner confirms access, because they are accountable for it.

exam_traps.trap: The review is complete once the owner signs it.
exam_traps.why: Signing is only the decision. The review is complete when every removal is carried out and visible in the system.

key_terms.definition: Approving every line of a review without really checking it.
An account unused for a set period; CIS Controls v8.1 advises disabling or deleting accounts inactive for 45 days.
One scheduled round of access reviews, sent to many reviewers with a deadline.

subtopics.name: Deprovisioning Leavers
subtopics.definition: Deprovisioning removes an identity's access when it is no longer needed: disabling accounts, revoking credentials and sessions, and collecting devices and badges.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Leftover accounts of former staff, contractors and vendors are a common route for misuse. Prompt removal also protects the former employee from being blamed for actions they did not take.
how_it_works: The HR exit record triggers removal; for a hostile exit, access is disabled before or as the person is told.
Disable the account first and delete it later under the retention policy, so logs and data stay traceable.
Revoke open sessions, tokens, remote access, certificates and MFA devices, not just the main password.
Change shared secrets the person knew, such as a shared social media or Wi-Fi password.
Collect laptops, badges and keys, and hand the person's data and owned service accounts to a new owner.
Contractors and vendors go through the same steps on their contract end date.
subtopics.example: A marketing agency ends a designer's contract on a Tuesday afternoon. Just before the meeting, Morgan, the IT technician, disables Kai's account and ends active sessions, as the exit checklist requires. After the meeting, Morgan collects Kai's laptop and badge, changes the shared social media password Kai used and records each step on the leaver ticket.

review: Work through the exit checklist in order and record each step
Change shared passwords the leaver knew, even after a friendly exit
evidence: Leaver report matched to disabled accounts and the time disabled
Accounts still active after their HR end date
audit_focus.recommend: Report any leaver account found active after the end date to the IAM team and the system owner at once.
audit_focus.decides: HR confirms the end date; the data owner decides what happens to the data

subtopics.isaca_rule: Remove access as fast as the risk demands: the same day as a rule, before the conversation for a hostile exit. Disable first and delete later, and cover everything the person could reach, not just one password.

exam_traps.trap: Delete the leaver's account immediately to be safe.
exam_traps.why: Deleting can lose data and the link between logs and the person. Disable at once, then delete under the retention policy.

exam_traps.trap: Disabling the main account removes all of a leaver's access.
exam_traps.why: Open sessions, API keys, remote access certificates and shared passwords can survive. Revoke each one and change shared secrets.

key_terms.definition: An exit where the person may be upset or likely to cause harm, so access is cut before or as they are told.
Rules for how long records and accounts are kept before secure deletion.
Ending a user's active sign-ins so open sessions stop working before they would expire.

subtopics.name: Non-Human Identities Through the Life Cycle
subtopics.definition: Non-human identities are accounts used by software rather than people, such as service accounts, bots, scripts, API keys and AI agents. They need the same life cycle as people.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Non-human identities often outnumber staff, hold broad rights and never resign on their own. The OWASP Top 10 for non-human identities ranks improper offboarding and leaked secrets as its top two risks.
how_it_works: Give every non-human identity a named human owner, a stated purpose and an entry in the inventory.
Give each workload or agent its own identity, never a shared or borrowed staff login.
Keep secrets in a vault, not in code or chat, and rotate them regularly and after any exposure.
Prefer short-lived, platform-issued tokens over long-lived keys where possible.
Review non-human access with its owner, and retire it when the owner leaves or the project ends.
Give each AI agent its own identity, scoped rights and logs of what it did.
subtopics.example: Months after a developer leaves a food delivery startup, its cloud bill spikes. An API key in the developer's old test script, still in a public code repository, is running someone else's workloads. Elif, a junior cloud engineer, revokes the key, reports the exposure to the security team and then starts an inventory of every key, its owner and its expiry date.

review: Inventory each service account, key and agent with its owner
Rotate any secret found in code, tickets or chat at once
evidence: Secret-scanning results for code repositories
Service accounts and keys with no recent use or no owner
audit_focus.recommend: Report exposed keys and ownerless service accounts to the security team and the system owner.
audit_focus.decides: The named owner decides whether a non-human identity is still needed

subtopics.isaca_rule: Treat every bot, key and agent like a worker with a badge: an owner, a purpose, only the access it needs and an end date. When the owner or the project leaves, the identity leaves too.

exam_traps.trap: Service accounts need no review because no person signs in with them.
exam_traps.why: They often hold broad, long-lived access that attackers target. Review them with their owner like any account.

exam_traps.trap: Letting an AI agent use a staff member's own login is simpler and just as safe.
exam_traps.why: The agent then gets all the person's rights and its actions look like theirs. Give it its own identity, scoped access and logs.

key_terms.definition: A secret string a program presents to prove which application is calling; anyone who copies it can use it.
A protected store that issues, rotates and logs use of system passwords, keys and tokens.
Software that uses an AI model to plan and take actions, such as calling tools or APIs, on someone's behalf.

subtopics.name: IAM Frameworks and Tools
subtopics.definition: IAM frameworks are published guides that describe good identity practice; IAM tools are the systems that carry it out, such as directories and identity governance platforms.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Frameworks give a shared, defensible standard, so practice does not rest on one person's opinion. Tools make the life cycle repeatable at scale and keep the records that reviews need.
how_it_works: NIST SP 800-63-4 covers digital identity: assurance levels for identity proofing, authentication and federation.
ISO/IEC 27002:2022 gives controls for identity management, authentication information, access rights and privileged access.
CIS Controls v8.1 Controls 5 and 6 give practical steps for account management and access control management.
NIST SP 800-207 describes Zero Trust, which checks identity and context on every request.
Tools connect: HR feeds identity governance, which creates directory accounts; the identity provider signs users in.

types.meaning: The central store of users, groups and their attributes that systems look up
Runs requests, approvals, provisioning and access reviews, and keeps the records
Guards administrator accounts with a vault, time-limited access and session logs

subtopics.example: A 40-person accounting firm tracks access in a spreadsheet, and two leavers kept email access for weeks. The office manager asks the new IT associate, Noor, for options. Noor maps the firm's steps against CIS Controls v8.1 Controls 5 and 6, lists the gaps and suggests linking the HR system to the cloud directory so starts and exits drive accounts. Noor presents the gap list to the office manager.

review: Map current IAM steps against one named framework to find gaps
Use the tool's records, not memory, as evidence of each change
evidence: Sample of recent starts and exits traced to directory changes
Connector logs showing HR changes reaching the directory
audit_focus.recommend: Present gaps and tool options to your manager, and leave the choice of framework and spending to leadership.
audit_focus.decides: Management chooses the framework, the tools and the budget for IAM

subtopics.isaca_rule: Frameworks say what good looks like; tools make it repeatable. Follow a recognized framework, drive the life cycle from a trusted source and keep the records that prove it works.

exam_traps.trap: Buying an IAM tool solves access problems by itself.
exam_traps.why: A tool automates whatever process it is given. Without defined roles, owners and reviews, it just automates the mess faster.

exam_traps.trap: A request from inside the office network can be trusted.
exam_traps.why: Zero Trust, described in NIST SP 800-207, checks identity and context on every request. Network location alone proves nothing.

key_terms.definition: A security approach that grants no trust for network location and checks every access request by identity and context.
How confident a system can be in a sign-in; NIST SP 800-63B-4 defines AAL1 to AAL3, with AAL3 the strongest.

topics.overview: Logical access controls are the software rules that decide what a signed-in identity may read, change or run. This topic covers the principles that set the limits (least privilege, need to know and separation of duties), the extra care privileged and automated accounts need, and the access control models that differ in who sets the rules: the owner, the system, roles, attributes or fixed rules.
can_do: Apply least privilege and need to know to choose the smallest access that still lets the work get done
Spot a separation of duties conflict and name a fitting fix or compensating control
Identify DAC, MAC, RBAC, ABAC and rule-based access control from a short scenario
Limit privileged, service and AI agent access with time limits, approval and logging

subtopics.name: Logical Access Controls and Access Decisions
subtopics.definition: Logical access controls are software rules that decide whether a subject, such as a user or process, may perform an action on an object, such as a file.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Once someone is signed in, these rules are what stop them reading payroll or deleting records they should not touch. Without them, strong authentication protects very little.
how_it_works: A subject (a user, process or AI agent) asks to perform an action (read, write, run or delete) on an object.
The system checks the permissions attached to the object, then allows or denies the request.
Anything not explicitly allowed is refused.
Grant permissions to groups or roles rather than individuals, so changes and reviews stay manageable.
Log access decisions, especially denials and permission changes, so misuse can be traced.
Logical controls are technical controls; they work beside physical controls, such as locks, and administrative ones, such as policy.
subtopics.example: At a small law firm, a paralegal, Jess, can open every client folder on the file server because the folders were shared with Everyone years ago. Sol, the IT assistant, notices this while setting up a new folder. Sol lists the open folders, suggests permissions by client team and sends the list to the managing partner, who owns the client files.

review: Remove direct grants to individuals and move them into groups
Look for Everyone or all-users permissions on sensitive data
evidence: Permission reports for folders that hold sensitive data
Logs of permission changes and denied access attempts
audit_focus.recommend: Report over-broad permissions on sensitive data to the data owner and the security team.
audit_focus.decides: The data owner sets which teams may open their files

subtopics.isaca_rule: Authentication says who you are; logical access controls say what you can touch. Start from default deny, grant through groups and let the data owner decide who gets in.

exam_traps.trap: Once users are authenticated, they can be trusted to open anything on the network.
exam_traps.why: Authentication only proves identity. Authorization rules still limit each identity to what its job needs.

key_terms.definition: The active party asking for access, such as a user, process, device or AI agent.
The resource being accessed, such as a file, database, printer or application.
A list attached to an object naming which subjects may access it and what each may do.
The rule that any access not explicitly allowed is refused; also called implicit deny.

subtopics.name: Least Privilege and Need to Know
subtopics.definition: Least privilege gives each user or process the minimum access its task needs, for as long as needed. Need to know limits information to people whose duties require it.
subtopics.why_it_matters: If an account is stolen or misused, least privilege limits the damage to what that account could reach. It also limits mistakes: nobody can delete what they cannot touch.
how_it_works: Start with no access and add only what the task requires.
Keep everyday and administrator accounts separate, so email and web browsing never run with admin rights.
Add time limits: temporary access ends automatically when the task is done.
Need to know is a second test: even someone cleared for sensitive data sees only the cases they work on.
Apply both to programs and AI agents: each gets only the data, tools and permissions its job needs.

rows.label: What it limits
cells: The actions a subject can perform
The information a person can see

rows.label: Question it asks
cells: What is the least this task can run with?
Does this person's current work require this data?

rows.label: Example
cells: A help desk agent can reset passwords but not change admin groups
A nurse sees records for patients in their care, not every patient

subtopics.example: A city council's parking app team asks for full administrator rights on the payments database to avoid delays. Taylor, a junior security analyst, asks what the app actually does: it reads fines and updates payment status. Taylor drafts a request for read access to the fines table and write access to the status field, and sends it to the database owner for approval.

review: Ask what the task actually does before granting any right
Use a separate administrator account for admin work only
evidence: Accounts with admin rights compared with their job needs
Temporary grants that are past their end date
audit_focus.recommend: Raise requests for broad or permanent rights with the data owner instead of approving them yourself.
audit_focus.decides: The data owner approves access beyond the standard role

subtopics.isaca_rule: When asked how much access to give, choose the smallest set that lets the work happen, and add an end date. Convenience and seniority are not reasons for more access.

exam_traps.trap: Senior managers should get broad access because of their position.
exam_traps.why: Rank is not a task. Senior accounts are prime targets, so they need least privilege as much as anyone.

exam_traps.trap: Being cleared for a classification level means seeing all data at that level.
exam_traps.why: Clearance is only the first test. Need to know limits a cleared person to the data their current work requires.

key_terms.definition: Gaining more rights than were granted, through a flaw or misconfiguration; least privilege limits what an attacker starts with.
Rights held all the time, whether or not they are in use; the opposite of time-limited access.

subtopics.memory_aid: Least privilege limits what you can do; need to know limits what you can see.

subtopics.name: Separation of Duties and Two-Person Control
subtopics.definition: Separation of duties (SoD) splits a sensitive task so no single person can complete it alone; two-person control requires two people to act together.
subtopics.why_it_matters: One person with end-to-end control can commit and hide fraud or a damaging mistake. Splitting duties means abuse needs collusion, two or more people agreeing to break the rules.
how_it_works: Separate who requests, who approves, who carries out and who checks, such as setting up a supplier and paying it.
Common conflicts: writing code and releasing it to production, granting access and reviewing it, raising and approving payments.
Check new roles and access requests for SoD conflicts before granting them.
Small teams that cannot split duties use compensating controls, such as logging and independent review.
Job rotation and required vacations help expose fraud one person might otherwise hide.

types.meaning: Two people must each act to finish a task, such as two approvals for a large transfer
Two authorized people must be present and act together, such as at a critical key ceremony
Each person holds only part of a secret, so nobody knows all of it

subtopics.example: At a nonprofit with three finance staff, the bookkeeper, Pat, can add new suppliers and also release payments. Hiring another person is not possible. Quinn, the part-time IT and security assistant, notes the conflict and proposes a compensating control to the finance director: a weekly report of new suppliers and payments, reviewed and signed by someone with no payment rights.

review: Compare each person's rights against a list of conflicting duties
Flag duties a small team cannot split, for the process owner
evidence: SoD conflict report from the access or finance system
Sign-off records for independent reviews of high-risk transactions
audit_focus.recommend: Report SoD conflicts to the process owner; never quietly give one person both duties.
audit_focus.decides: The process owner splits the duties or accepts a compensating control

subtopics.isaca_rule: No single person should be able to start, approve and hide a sensitive action. Split the duties; where the team is too small, add independent review. Controls should not depend on trusting one good employee.

exam_traps.trap: Separation of duties and least privilege are the same thing.
exam_traps.why: Least privilege limits how much one person can do. SoD splits a process so it needs more than one person. Someone can hold minimal rights and still have a conflict.

exam_traps.trap: A trusted, long-serving employee can safely hold conflicting duties.
exam_traps.why: SoD is not about distrust of one person. It protects the organization, and the employee, from fraud and from suspicion.

key_terms.definition: Two or more people secretly working together to get around a control such as separation of duties.
An alternative control that reduces the risk when the preferred control is not possible.
Moving people between duties on a schedule, so hidden misuse is more likely to come to light.

subtopics.name: Privileged Access Management
subtopics.definition: Privileged access management controls accounts that can change systems, security settings or other users' access, such as administrator, root and database owner accounts.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Privileged accounts are the keys attackers want most, because one compromise can switch off defenses or reach everything. Mistakes made with admin rights also have the widest impact.
how_it_works: Keep a full inventory of privileged accounts, including built-in admin, service and cloud console accounts.
Each administrator uses a separate, named admin account for admin work only, never a shared one.
Grant admin rights just in time, for a set task and period, with approval.
Store admin credentials in a vault that checks them out, rotates them and logs each use.
Require phishing-resistant MFA, and record or log privileged sessions for review.
Keep sealed emergency accounts for when normal sign-in fails, and alert on every use.
subtopics.example: At a manufacturing plant, five engineers share one password for the production servers' admin account, unchanged for three years. When an overnight change stops the line, nobody can tell who made it. Fatima, a junior security analyst, documents the gap and drafts a proposal for named admin accounts, a vault with check-out and session logs, and sends it to the plant's systems owner.

review: Inventory every account with admin or root rights, including built-in ones
Use your own admin account only for admin tasks
evidence: Change tickets matched to each privileged sign-in
Privileged accounts without MFA or outside the vault
audit_focus.recommend: Report shared or unvaulted admin accounts to the system owner and the security team.
audit_focus.decides: The system owner approves who holds privileged access and for how long

subtopics.isaca_rule: The more power an account has, the tighter its controls: named accounts, phishing-resistant MFA, time-limited grants, a vault and recorded sessions. Sharing an admin password for convenience is not acceptable.

exam_traps.trap: Give each administrator permanent admin rights so they can respond quickly.
exam_traps.why: Standing rights are available to an attacker too. Just-in-time grants and emergency accounts give speed without permanent exposure.

exam_traps.trap: Sharing one admin password is fine if only trusted engineers know it.
exam_traps.why: A shared account cannot show who acted and must be changed whenever anyone leaves. Use named admin accounts through a vault.

key_terms.definition: Privileges granted only when needed, for a set task and time, then removed automatically.
A sealed emergency account used only when normal admin access fails, with every use alerted and reviewed.
Capturing what an administrator does during a privileged session, so actions can be reviewed later.

subtopics.name: Discretionary Access Control (DAC)
subtopics.definition: Discretionary access control (DAC) lets the owner of a resource, usually its creator, decide who else may access it and what they may do.
subtopics.why_it_matters: DAC is how most file shares, cloud documents and personal folders work. It is flexible, but it rests on each owner's judgment, so sensitive data can be overshared with one click.
how_it_works: The owner sets permissions on their own files, often through an access control list.
Depending on the rights given, people the owner shares with may be able to share again.
Everyday examples: sharing a cloud document by link, or setting permissions on a personal folder.
Weaknesses: inconsistent decisions, oversharing, and malware that runs with the user's rights and so gets their access.
Organizations limit DAC with policy, sharing restrictions, data labels and access reviews.
subtopics.example: A project lead at a design studio, Robin, shares a client contract folder with a freelance illustrator using an anyone-with-the-link setting. The link later appears on a public forum. Ezra, the studio's IT assistant, gets the sharing alert, switches the folder to named people only and reports the exposure to the studio manager, following the incident procedure.

review: Review sharing settings on folders that hold sensitive data
Replace open link sharing with access for named people
evidence: Sharing reports listing files shared externally or by link
The owner recorded for each shared folder
audit_focus.recommend: Report sensitive data shared outside the organization to the data owner, following the incident procedure.
audit_focus.decides: The data owner decides who may see the data, within policy

subtopics.isaca_rule: In DAC the owner decides. That flexibility is both its strength and its weakness, so pair DAC with sharing limits, labels and reviews when the data is sensitive.

exam_traps.trap: Under DAC, a central administrator decides who gets access.
exam_traps.why: Central decisions describe non-discretionary models such as RBAC or MAC. In DAC the resource owner decides.

exam_traps.trap: DAC is the most secure model because owners know their data best.
exam_traps.why: Owners can overshare by mistake, and malware inherits their rights. DAC is the most flexible model, not the strictest.

key_terms.definition: The person or account that owns a file or other object and, under DAC, controls who can use it.
Giving access to anyone who holds a web link to a file; convenient but easy to forward.

subtopics.memory_aid: DAC: the owner's Discretion. MAC: the system's Mandate.

subtopics.name: Mandatory Access Control (MAC)
subtopics.definition: Mandatory access control (MAC) lets the system, not the owner, decide access by comparing a subject's clearance with the object's classification label under central policy.
subtopics.why_it_matters: MAC protects highly sensitive data where one user's choice must never be able to leak it, such as in military, government and intelligence systems.
how_it_works: Every object carries a security label, such as Confidential, Secret or Top Secret.
Every subject has a clearance, set by a central security authority.
Access is allowed only when the clearance is high enough and the person also has a need to know.
Users cannot change labels or pass data to a lower level, even for files they created.
MAC is strong but rigid and costly to run, so it suits high-security settings more than everyday business.
subtopics.example: At a defense contractor, an engineer, Lin, cleared to Secret, works on a design file labeled Secret. Lin tries to paste part of it into an unclassified email to a supplier, and the system blocks it; Lin cannot change the label. Instead of looking for a workaround, Lin asks the security officer to review the extract for an authorized release.

review: Follow the labeling procedure when creating or handling data
Request a formal review before any data moves to a lower level
evidence: Denied access events showing label and clearance mismatches
Records of who changed labels or clearances, and who approved
audit_focus.recommend: Report attempts to bypass labels or clearances to the security officer straight away.
audit_focus.decides: The central security officer sets labels, clearances and releases

subtopics.isaca_rule: In MAC the system enforces central policy, and nobody, not even the creator, can override it. When a scenario says users cannot change permissions and access follows labels and clearances, think MAC.

exam_traps.trap: The creator of a file can share it under MAC because they own it.
exam_traps.why: Ownership gives no control in MAC. Labels and clearances, set centrally, decide access.

exam_traps.trap: A Top Secret clearance opens every Top Secret file.
exam_traps.why: MAC also checks need to know, often through compartments. Clearance is necessary but not enough.

key_terms.definition: A classification marking attached to an object, such as Secret, that the system reads to decide access.
The highest classification level a person is approved to access, granted after vetting.
A named category within a classification, such as a project, that adds a need-to-know check on top of clearance.

subtopics.name: Role-Based Access Control (RBAC)
subtopics.definition: Role-based access control (RBAC) attaches permissions to roles that match job functions, then assigns people to roles, so access follows the job rather than the person.
subtopics.why_it_matters: RBAC is the most common model in business systems because it scales. Changing someone's job means changing their role, and reviewing a role reviews everyone in it at once.
how_it_works: Permissions attach to roles, such as Nurse, Pharmacist or Billing clerk; people are assigned roles.
A person can hold several roles, and their permissions add together, which can create conflicts.
Policy can stop one person holding conflicting roles, such as Requester and Approver.
Movers change roles and leavers lose all roles, so life cycle events map neatly onto RBAC.
RBAC weakens when custom roles multiply or permissions are granted outside any role.
subtopics.example: A clinic's records system grants access by role. When a receptionist, Elena, finishes training as a medical assistant, the practice manager approves the change. Hana, the IT coordinator, removes Elena's Receptionist role and assigns the Medical Assistant role. Elena's access changes in minutes, and Hana confirms no one-off permissions are left over from the old job.

review: Assign access by role, not by copying another user
Compare each person's combined roles with the conflict list
evidence: Membership lists for each sensitive role
Direct grants that bypass the role catalog
audit_focus.recommend: Report one-off permissions or conflicting roles to the role owner for a decision.
audit_focus.decides: The role owner approves what a role contains and who holds it

subtopics.isaca_rule: When access follows the job and changes when the job changes, think RBAC. It is non-discretionary: the organization defines the roles, and users cannot hand out rights themselves.

exam_traps.trap: RBAC lets each user decide who joins their role.
exam_traps.why: Role membership is set by the organization through an approved process. That central control is what makes RBAC non-discretionary.

exam_traps.trap: RBAC on its own can allow or block access by time of day or location.
exam_traps.why: Plain RBAC checks only the role. Decisions on time, location or data sensitivity need rules or attributes, as in rule-based access control or ABAC.

key_terms.definition: A named set of permissions that matches a job function, such as Accounts Clerk.
Roles that policy forbids one person to hold together, such as Requester and Approver.

subtopics.name: Attribute-Based Access Control (ABAC)
subtopics.definition: Attribute-based access control (ABAC) decides each request by checking a policy against attributes of the user, the resource, the action and the environment, such as time or location.
subtopics.why_it_matters: ABAC handles fine-grained, changing conditions that roles alone cannot, such as letting managers approve expenses only for their own region, in business hours, from a managed device.
how_it_works: Subject attributes describe the user: department, clearance, job title or training completed.
Object attributes describe the resource: data classification, owner, project or region.
Environment attributes describe the moment: time, location, device health or current threat level.
A policy engine checks each request against the policy, so access changes as attributes change, without new roles.
ABAC needs accurate, trusted attributes and careful testing; one wrong attribute changes the answer.
NIST SP 800-162 describes ABAC, and Zero Trust designs often use it for per-request decisions.
subtopics.example: An international charity's grant files must be readable only by staff in the same country office, on managed laptops. A role for every country and device type would mean hundreds of roles. Omar, a junior cloud administrator, helps the IAM lead build an ABAC policy using the user's country, the file's country tag and device status, and tests it with sample accounts before release.

review: Test each policy with sample users before it goes live
Report wrong or missing attributes at their source
evidence: Policy test results for both allowed and denied cases
Attribute source records, such as the HR department field
audit_focus.recommend: Report a policy that grants unexpected access to the policy owner before it is used.
audit_focus.decides: The data owner and the security team approve the access policies

subtopics.isaca_rule: When a scenario combines several conditions, such as who, what, where and when, think ABAC. Its decisions are only as good as its attributes, so the HR and asset data behind it must be correct.

exam_traps.trap: ABAC is just RBAC with more roles.
exam_traps.why: ABAC does not need a role for each case. It checks attributes on every request, so one policy can cover many combinations.

exam_traps.trap: Once the policy is written correctly, ABAC cannot grant the wrong access.
exam_traps.why: ABAC trusts its attributes. A stale department field in the HR system can grant or block access wrongly.

key_terms.definition: A characteristic used in an access decision, such as department, data label, location or time.
The component that checks each request against the access policy and returns allow or deny.

subtopics.name: Rule-Based Access Control
subtopics.definition: Rule-based access control applies fixed rules, set by an administrator, to every subject alike, such as firewall rules or a ban on sign-ins outside business hours.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Rules enforce broad limits regardless of who the user is, which suits network traffic and time or location limits. Confusing rule-based with role-based control is a common exam slip.
how_it_works: An administrator writes the rules, and the system applies them to every request that matches.
Rules are usually checked in order, the first match decides, and a final rule denies everything else.
Typical uses: firewall and router access lists, time-of-day limits and blocking sign-ins from certain countries.
Users cannot change the rules, so it is a non-discretionary model.
Rules often sit on top of another model: RBAC sets what a nurse can do, and a rule limits it to clinic devices.
subtopics.example: A payroll system is used only during office hours, yet its logs show sign-in attempts at 3 a.m. Avery, a junior network administrator, submits a change through change management and, once approved, adds a rule blocking payroll sign-ins from 8 p.m. to 6 a.m., except for the on-call payroll group. Avery then checks the logs to confirm the rule works.

review: Submit rule changes through change management with a rollback plan
Confirm the last rule denies anything not already allowed
evidence: Rule list showing an owner and purpose for each rule
Hit counts showing which rules are used and which never match
audit_focus.recommend: Report rules nobody can explain to the rule owner instead of deleting them yourself.
audit_focus.decides: The network or system owner approves each rule and its removal

subtopics.isaca_rule: The same administrator-written rule for everyone: think rule-based. Access that depends on the person's job: think role-based. When options mix them up, ask whether access depends on the job or on a condition.

exam_traps.trap: Rule-based and role-based access control are the same model.
exam_traps.why: Role-based ties permissions to job roles. Rule-based applies the same administrator-written conditions, such as time or address, to everyone.

exam_traps.trap: Rules can be added freely, since each one only allows a little.
exam_traps.why: Rules pile up and interact. Unreviewed rules leave gaps, so each needs an owner, a purpose and periodic review.

key_terms.definition: An ordered instruction that allows or blocks traffic by address, port or protocol.
A final rule that blocks anything earlier rules did not allow, putting default deny into practice.
Any model where central policy, not the resource owner, decides access; MAC, RBAC and rule-based models are usually grouped here.

subtopics.name: Choosing an Access Control Model
subtopics.definition: Choosing an access control model starts with one question: who or what decides access, the owner, labels, job roles, attributes or fixed rules, and does it fit the risk?
subtopics.why_it_matters: Exam scenarios rarely name the model; they describe who decides and what the decision depends on. Real organizations also mix models, so knowing where each fits avoids a poor choice.
how_it_works: Ask first who decides: the owner points to DAC, central labels to MAC and job roles to RBAC.
Ask next what it depends on: several conditions at once point to ABAC, one fixed condition for everyone to rule-based.
Match the model to the data: personal and team files suit DAC, classified data suits MAC, most businesses use RBAC.
Combine models where it helps, such as RBAC for applications, DAC for personal folders and rules on the firewall.

rows.label: DAC
cells: The resource owner
Small teams, personal and shared files
Oversharing; malware gets the user's rights

rows.label: MAC
cells: The system, using labels and clearances
Classified or highly sensitive data
Rigid and costly to run

rows.label: RBAC
cells: The organization, through job roles
Most business applications
Role explosion and copied access

rows.label: ABAC
cells: A policy over many attributes
Fine-grained, changing conditions
Complexity; depends on accurate attributes

rows.label: Rule-based
cells: Administrator rules, the same for all
Firewalls, time and location limits
Rule sprawl; confusion with role-based

subtopics.example: A veterinary chain of 12 clinics gives each new hire whatever their predecessor had. Avi, the junior IT analyst, notices that staff fall into five job types and suggests RBAC, plus a rule blocking sign-ins to the drug inventory system outside clinic hours. Avi writes up both options, with the risks each one reduces, and presents them to the operations director.

review: Identify who decides, and on what, before naming a model
Record which model each major system uses
evidence: Each system's access settings showing owner, role or rule decisions
Exceptions where users hold access outside the chosen model
audit_focus.recommend: Bring proposals to change a system's model to the system owner and the security team for a decision.
audit_focus.decides: Management and system owners choose the model, based on risk

subtopics.isaca_rule: Read the scenario for the decider. The owner chooses: DAC. Labels and clearances: MAC. The job: RBAC. Many conditions: ABAC. One rule for all: rule-based. Then choose the model that fits the risk, not the strictest one.

exam_traps.trap: Pick MAC every time, because the strictest model is the most secure.
exam_traps.why: MAC is rigid and costly. The best model fits the data's sensitivity and the organization's needs; most businesses use RBAC.

exam_traps.trap: An organization must use one model for everything.
exam_traps.why: Mixing is normal: roles for applications, owner sharing for personal folders and rules on network devices.

key_terms.definition: A formal approach that sets who or what decides access, such as DAC, MAC, RBAC or ABAC.
Using more than one access control model in one organization, each where it fits best.

subtopics.name: Least Privilege and SoD for Automated Systems and AI Agents
subtopics.definition: Applying least privilege and separation of duties to automation means scripts, bots and AI agents get only the access their task needs and cannot finish high-risk actions alone.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Automation acts fast and at scale, so an over-privileged bot or a manipulated AI agent can do damage in seconds. The OWASP Top 10 for large language model (LLM) applications calls this risk excessive agency.
how_it_works: Scope each bot or agent to the data, tools and actions its task needs.
An agent acting for a person never gets more than that person's rights.
Keep a human approval step for high-impact actions, such as payments, deletions or access changes.
One automation should not both make a change and approve it.
Log every action under the agent's own identity, and keep a quick way to stop it.
Treat instructions inside emails, files or web pages as untrusted input.
subtopics.example: A property management firm pilots an AI agent that reads tenant emails and books repairs. The vendor's setup asks for full access to the finance system for future features. Wren, a junior security analyst, maps what the agent actually does and sends the system owner a proposal: read access to the repair calendar, write access to work orders only and a manager's approval for any payment the agent drafts.

review: List each action an agent or bot takes, then grant only those
Test that the agent stops and waits at each approval step
evidence: The agent's permission list compared with its documented tasks
Logs of actions taken under the agent's own identity
audit_focus.recommend: Report an agent or bot with broad or unexplained rights to its owner and the security team.
audit_focus.decides: The system owner decides what an automated system may do without a person

subtopics.isaca_rule: Automation follows the same rules as people, applied more strictly because it acts faster: its own identity, least privilege, no end-to-end control of risky actions, full logs and a way to stop it.

exam_traps.trap: An AI agent is just software, so access control principles do not apply to it.
exam_traps.why: An agent acts like a user: it reads data and takes actions. It needs its own identity, scoped rights and oversight.

exam_traps.trap: Broad access for an AI agent is safe when the vendor is reputable.
exam_traps.why: Broad access lets a manipulated or faulty agent cause wide harm. Grant per task; a good vendor does not shrink what the access allows.

key_terms.definition: An AI system given more functions, permissions or independence than its task needs, so a bad output can cause harm.
A design where a person must review or approve an automated action before it takes effect.
Crafted or hidden instructions in input that make an AI model ignore its original instructions.

key_terminologies.Identity: The record that represents one person or system across the organization.
key_terminologies.Identification: Claiming an identity, such as by entering a username; it proves nothing on its own.
key_terminologies.Authentication: Proving a claimed identity with one or more factors.
key_terminologies.Authorization: Deciding what an authenticated identity may do.
key_terminologies.Identity life cycle: The joiner, mover and leaver stages an identity passes through, with reviews alongside.
key_terminologies.Provisioning: Creating an account and granting its approved access.
key_terminologies.Deprovisioning: Removing an identity's access, credentials and sessions when they are no longer needed.
key_terminologies.Access review: A regular check by a manager or owner that each account and right is still needed.
key_terminologies.Privilege creep: The buildup of unneeded access as people change jobs and keep old rights.
key_terminologies.Multi-factor authentication (MFA): Sign-in that combines at least two different factor categories: know, have or are.
key_terminologies.Phishing-resistant authentication: Sign-in tied to the genuine site, such as passkeys and FIDO2 keys, that a fake page cannot reuse.
key_terminologies.Single sign-on (SSO): One sign-in at an identity provider that gives access to many applications.
key_terminologies.Federation: Trust between organizations or systems that lets one accept the other's sign-ins.
key_terminologies.Adaptive authentication: Sign-in checks that rise or fall with the risk score of each attempt.
key_terminologies.Least privilege: Giving each identity only the access its task needs, for only as long as needed.
key_terminologies.Need to know: Limiting information to people whose current duties require it.
key_terminologies.Separation of duties (SoD): Splitting a sensitive process so no single person can complete it alone.
key_terminologies.Privileged account: An account that can change systems, security settings or other users' access.
key_terminologies.Service account: An account used by an application or process rather than a person.
key_terminologies.Non-human identity: Any identity used by software, such as a service account, bot, API key or AI agent.
key_terminologies.Discretionary access control (DAC): The resource owner decides who may access it.
key_terminologies.Mandatory access control (MAC): The system decides access by comparing clearances with classification labels.
key_terminologies.Role-based access control (RBAC): Permissions attach to job roles, and people are assigned roles.
key_terminologies.Attribute-based access control (ABAC): A policy decides each request using attributes of the user, resource, action and environment.
key_terminologies.Rule-based access control: Administrator-written rules apply the same way to every subject.
